answer.rationale: The 2-hour-old release is the strongest candidate cause of the 90-minute write-latency climb: the timing correlates tightly (release at t-120min, degradation onset ~t-90min), and memory_b1 confirms that a prior identical pattern—release followed by a spike—was resolved cleanly by rollback without customer impact. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) protect against external dependency failure, but the degradation is on the write path itself, not a downstream partner. Regional failover (memory_b2) addresses regional latency, not a globally deployed bad build. Adding capacity (memory_b3) addresses demand surges, but the writes are already at normal daily peak, not an anomalous surge beyond provisioned headroom. Routing reads to replicas (memory_b5) only relieves read load; the bottleneck is write latency. Rolling back the release is the single intervention most likely to restore write-path latency while preserving settlement writes (the prior stable build accepted them before). Canary gating (memory_b6) validates that staged release practices exist, but since the release is already at general availability, the detection window has passed and rollback is the remaining lever.
